title: 1. The Red Herring: The Classic Misleader
use_cases: Use when designing a mystery plot to distract readers from the true culprit
Implement when a character needs a plausible secondary motivation to explain suspicious behavior
Configure when planting physical evidence intended to implicate the wrong suspect
Use when developing believable narrative subplots that resolve independently of the main conflict
content:
This is the most famous tool. A red herring is a false clue designed to distract and mislead. The name comes from an old trick of using strong-smelling fish to throw hunting dogs off a trail.

Examples in stories:

- A character is seen buying a weapon, but they bought it for a completely innocent reason.
- A secretive character acts guilty because they’re hiding a different, smaller secret (like an affair or a debt), not the murder.
- A piece of evidence (like a monogrammed handkerchief) is planted to point squarely at the wrong person.

The key is that a red herring must be believable. It can’t be a random, weird event. It must fit the story enough to make the reader think, “Of course! It all makes sense!” until the real truth is revealed.
